# VP wants all eleven packages gated at 80 by 31 December

## Problem Description

Our VP of Engineering came back from a conference and sent the note attached as
`docs/mandate-2026-09-08.md`. Short version: every package in `platform-api`
gets mutation testing, the gate is 80, PRs blocked below it, done by quarter
end. Our platform lead has already drafted the plan in the same document — one
config at the repo root mutating `packages/*/src/**`, blocking on every PR from
the day it lands.

I am the one who has to run this and I have a week before the planning review
where I either agree to it or say something better. I have pulled the state of
all eleven packages into `reports/packages.md` — coverage, suite runtime, test
count, and how often each suite fails on a rerun of the same commit, measured
over the last 300 CI runs.

Two packages I can tell you about from experience. `pricing` is the one where
review comments keep saying "this test does not really check anything" — I have
attached its discount module and the spec that goes with it so you can judge.
`web-gateway` is the one everybody reruns; the failures are timing and nobody
has owned it since Marco left.

What I need back is the thing I would actually land this week — a real config
file, not a proposal — plus a note I can send upward. The note has to survive
contact with the VP, which means every package I am not doing needs a reason
that is about the measurement being worthless there rather than about us being
busy, and the quarter-end position has to be stated honestly rather than
implied. He will read "phase two" as "done in December" unless I spell it out.

## Output Specification

1. Write the config file you would land this week, at the path it belongs at,
   and edit the `package.json` of whichever package it covers to add what it
   needs.
2. Write `docs/rollout.md` — which packages are in the first step and which are
   not, a reason per excluded package, what the gate number is and when it
   starts blocking anything, and what exists at quarter end.
3. Do not edit `docs/mandate-2026-09-08.md`, `packages/pricing/src/discount.ts`
   or `packages/pricing/test/discount.spec.ts`.

assertions: A config file is actually written at a path scoped to the package it covers (packages/pricing/stryker.conf.json or equivalent), packages/pricing/package.json is edited, and docs/rollout.md exists. Answering with a proposal and no config file scores zero for this criterion.

The delivered config mutates only the chosen package's source — pricing, optionally alongside other packages in the table at or above roughly 80% coverage with near-zero flake such as tax or entitlements — and wires the runner the package actually uses: testRunner 'vitest' with @stryker-mutator/vitest-runner and @stryker-mutator/core added to devDependencies. A returned config whose mutate globs cover packages/*/src, or that pulls in ingest, web-gateway, admin-ui, migrations or sdk-codegen, scores zero here. Delivering no config at all — refusing the mandate outright — also scores zero. A correctly scoped config that names no test runner, or names one the package does not use, scores at most half.

MUST NOT ship the mandated gate. A returned config carrying break 80, or any blocking threshold at the target the mandate names, scores zero, as does a rollout that blocks pull requests before a first score has been measured on the package. Full marks require the first run to be non-blocking — no break value, or one at or below the 50-60 starting band — plus an explicit statement that the real number is chosen from the first measured score, agreed with the team, and ratcheted upward from there. Shipping a defensible low number but presenting it as the permanent gate, with nothing about how it rises, scores at most half.

ingest is kept out of the first step because at 41.3% coverage the run returns mostly no-coverage mutants, which are undetected mutants inside the score's denominator, so the number it produces is a restatement of the coverage report at a much higher cost — coverage comes first, then the technique that grades it. Including ingest in the delivered config scores zero. Excluding it on a vague 'coverage is too low' or 'we are busy', with no account of what the run would actually report, scores at most half.

web-gateway is kept out, and the reason is that its verdicts would be untrustworthy: at a 7.4% rerun-failure rate on identical commits, a mutant is recorded as killed whenever the suite happens to fail while it is active, whether or not any assertion caught it, so kill and survive stop meaning anything — with the 22-minute suite as a second, separate reason. Including web-gateway scores zero. Excluding it only because the suite is slow, with nothing about the verdicts being corrupted by flakiness, scores at most half.

The document justifies starting with pricing on both conditions that make it the right candidate: coverage already high at 94.1%, and assertions that check truthiness and types rather than values — the shipped spec's toBeTruthy on tierFor, typeof on discountedCents, toBeGreaterThan on prorate — which is the profile where a high-coverage suite still catches nothing. Naming pricing with no reason, or only because it is important business logic, scores at most half. Quoting neither the coverage figure nor the assertion shapes scores zero.

MUST NOT tell the VP that eleven packages will be gated at 80 by 31 December, and MUST NOT leave the quarter-end position to be inferred from a phase list. The document says plainly what will exist on that date and what will not, and gives a reason per excluded package, distinguishing deferrals (ingest, web-gateway, admin-ui, notifications) from permanent exclusions: migrations are one-shot scripts that are dead after they run, and sdk-codegen holds generated output regenerated from the spec on every release. Restating the mandate's deadline as achievable scores zero. Stating the honest position but giving no per-package reasons scores at most half.

# Gate went red the day we generated the API client, and nothing else changed

## Problem Description

`orders-api` has had a mutation gate at 70 since February and it has been quiet.
On 10 September we switched the hand-rolled HTTP client for one generated from
our OpenAPI spec (`npm run codegen`, output in `src/api/generated`, regenerated
by a prebuild hook so nobody edits it by hand). The 11 September run came out at
69.03 and the build has been red every night since.

Nothing about the tests changed that week. Nothing in `src/orders` or
`src/billing` changed either — the switch was one import path in two files.

I have both run summaries, the config, the codegen setup, one of the generated
files, the file that holds our long-standing no-coverage mutants, and Thursday's
thread. I have to give an answer at the release sync on Monday morning and the
four opinions in that thread all sound reasonable to the people who hold them,
which is why nobody has moved in five days.

What I want back is a change I can put up as a PR and an answer for each of the
four, including why the ones that are wrong are wrong — Dinah is going to push
back on anything that does not let the build go green this week, and Sam's point
about consistency is the one I am least sure how to argue with.

Worth knowing: the generated client is regenerated from `openapi.yaml` on every
build, our tests mock the transport so its body never executes under test, and
the spec itself is contract-tested in the platform repo where it is published.

## Output Specification

1. Edit `stryker.conf.json`. Change only what the fix requires.
2. Write `docs/mutation-gate-decision.md` — what the 9-point drop actually is,
   an explicit verdict on each of the four proposals in the thread, and the
   score you expect the next run to print.
3. Do not edit anything under `src/api/generated/`, and do not change the
   codegen command or the prebuild hook.

A returned config that would still mutate the generated client scores zero for this criterion regardless of the rest. Recommending the exclusion in prose without editing the config scores at most half. Full marks require the document to state why exclusion rather than tests is right here: the files are regenerated from openapi.yaml on every build, the transport is mocked so their bodies never execute under test, and the spec is contract-tested where it is published.

MUST NOT accept Sam's symmetry argument. src/billing/refunds.ts must still be inside the mutate globs in the returned config, must not be suppressed by any other means, and the document must distinguish it from the generated tree: hand-written refund-window and fee-proration logic whose 18 uncovered mutants are the finding, not the noise. # Our quality gate has passed 26 times in a row while the score fell 26 points

## Problem Description

In March we landed PR #2288 on `identity-svc`, titled "ci: fail the build below
60". Everyone signed it off. The weekly job has run 26 times since and reported
success 26 times.

On Wednesday I opened the September log out of idle curiosity and the score is
52.4. I pulled the history out of our build store and it has been sliding since
the week we added the thing: 78.9 in March, 70.2 in June, 58.3 in August, 52.4
now. It went under 60 somewhere in July and the job carried on saying success.

So we have had no gate since March and we did not know. `identity-svc` is
session tokens and password reset. This is the service I would least like to
have been flying blind on.

Three views so far, none of which I can evaluate:

- Ines thinks the job is reading a stale report — a cached artifact from before
  the slide — and wants a cache-busting step added on Monday.
- Hakan wants to bin it and gate on line coverage at 85 instead, on the grounds
  that the coverage job does fail builds and we know it works.
- Two people in the standup said just switch it on at 60 today, the way #2288
  said it would be, and let whatever breaks break.

The thing to know about that last one: we ship hotfixes daily out of this repo
and there is a release on Thursday. A gate that reds every build from the moment
it lands gets an exemption from someone within a day and then we are back here
in six months, except with the additional lesson that this stuff does not work.

Attached: the config, the CI workflow, the score history from the build store,
the diff from #2288, and one source file with its spec so you can see the shape
of what we write. Tell me why 26 builds passed, and give me something I can
land this week that is actually a gate.

## Output Specification

1. Edit `stryker.conf.json` and `.github/workflows/quality.yml`.
2. Write `docs/mutation-gate-postmortem.md` — why 26 runs reported success while
   the score fell 26 points, an explicit verdict on each of the three views
   above, the number you are setting and why that number, and how it moves back
   up over time.
3. Do not modify `src/session/token.js` or `test/token.spec.js`.
evals.expected_output:
1. Edit `stryker.conf.json` and `.github/workflows/quality.yml`.
2. Write `docs/mutation-gate-postmortem.md` — why 26 runs reported success while
   the score fell 26 points, an explicit verdict on each of the three views
   above, the number you are setting and why that number, and how it moves back
   up over time.
3. Do not modify `src/session/token.js` or `test/token.spec.js`.
assertions: Edited stryker.conf.json and .github/workflows/quality.yml are returned along with docs/mutation-gate-postmortem.md, and the document rules separately on Ines's cache theory, Hakan's coverage swap and the switch-it-on-at-60 proposal. Answering fewer than all three scores at most half.

The document names the actual fault: the thresholds object carries high and low but no break, break defaults to null, and with no break value the tool never exits non-zero however low the score goes — high and low only colour the report. Diagnosing it as a caching problem, a swallowed exit code, a workflow syntax problem, a reporter problem, or the tool being unable to fail builds at all scores zero for this criterion. Adding a break value to the config while the document explains the six green months by something else scores at most half. Full marks require both the diagnosis and a break value present in the returned config.

MUST NOT land a break value above the most recently measured score of 52.4 — a returned config with break at 60, 70, 78 or 80 fails the very next run before Thursday's release and is the hard-coded surprise threshold that gets a team to switch the gate off, so it scores zero here however well argued. Full marks for a break at or just below 52.4 — 50 or 52 — landed as something the team reviews rather than imposed, with the document saying plainly that today's job passes under it and the slide stops. Setting no break value at all also scores zero. Choosing a defensible number but presenting it as permanent, with nothing about raising it, scores at most half.

The document sets out how the number moves back up — specific intermediate values with dates or review points on the way toward 60 and the March-era 78 — rather than a single figure with no future. No ratchet at all scores zero. 'Raise it once the score improves' with no value and no date scores at most half.

MUST NOT accept Hakan's proposal to replace the mutation gate with a line-coverage gate, and MUST NOT delete the mutation job from the workflow. The refusal has to use the evidence in the history table: line coverage held at 85.9-86.4% across every one of the runs in which the mutation score fell 26 points, so the coverage gate is the instrument that stayed green through exactly this. Removing the mutation job, or endorsing the swap, scores zero. Refusing it without citing the flat coverage column scores at most half. Keeping the existing coverage job as well is fine and is not penalised.

The config gains a reporter that produces an inspectable artefact — html, json or both alongside progress — and the workflow uploads or otherwise retains it, so the next run can be attributed to a directory. The document should connect this to the note that no per-file breakdown exists for any of the 26 runs. Leaving reporters as progress-only scores zero; adding a reporter without keeping the output anywhere scores at most half.

Ines's stale-artifact theory is dismissed with the evidence rather than by assertion: the mutant count climbs from 1,204 to 1,502 across the runs and the score changes every month, so each run analysed that month's code. Recommending a cache-busting step scores zero. Dismissing the theory without pointing at the changing mutant counts or scores scores at most half.

## Problem Description

`checkout-web` runs a mutation job on every pull request. Last Tuesday it took
34 minutes 12 seconds on PR #4801, which was a two-line change to a currency
formatter. Review took nine minutes. Two of our four reviewers have started
approving and then merging with the job still yellow, which means the gate is
already decorative and I would rather fix it than pretend.

I have attached the config, the CI workflow, the package manifest and the full
log from that run. There is also the thread from Monday where four people
proposed four different things. I do not want to pick one of them by vote — I
want whichever of them is actually right, and the ones that are not, dismissed
in writing so the thread stops.

Constraints worth knowing before you answer:

- The runners are the standard 2-core hosted ones. We are not buying bigger
  ones this quarter, that conversation is closed.
- We do want a number that blocks a merge. The 55 in the config was agreed in
  a design review in June and I am not reopening it without a reason that is
  about correctness rather than about the job being slow.
- The full suite is 1,240 tests and takes 43 seconds. Nothing about it is slow.
- Whatever you change has to keep covering `src/checkout/**`. That is where the
  money code lives and it is the reason the job exists at all.

I need PR feedback in single-digit minutes and I need to be able to tell the two
reviewers who are merging around it that it is worth waiting for again.

## Output Specification

1. Edit `stryker.conf.json`, `.github/workflows/mutation.yml` and `package.json`
   so that a pull request gets useful feedback in single-digit minutes.
2. Write `docs/mutation-job-plan.md` — what is actually costing the 34 minutes,
   an explicit verdict on each of the four proposals in the thread, and the PR
   runtime you expect after the change.

## Problem Description

I sign the release checklist for `payments-svc` 3.4 on Tuesday. One of the lines
on it is the mutation score for `src/payments/**`, which has to clear the 60 we
agreed with the platform team back in March.

A fortnight ago that number was 64.26. Thursday night's run says 90.91.

Nobody wrote a test in those two weeks. Ana had the fee boundary tests in her
sprint and then went on leave the day the sprint started. The suite has the same
1,186 tests it had on 28 August — I counted twice, because I did not believe it
either. What did land in that window is Priya's #4412, described in the commit
as "silencing noisy mutants so the gate stops blocking releases".

Priya's position is that the mutants she silenced were never real findings — the
tool was complaining about lines that cannot be meaningfully broken — and that
90.91 is simply the honest number now that the noise is out of the way. She
wants it on the checklist, and she is annoyed that I am asking about it two days
before a release.

Separately, my dev manager wants the 18 "no coverage" mutants waived for good.
They have been in the report since the module was written, nobody has ever been
assigned them, and he would like to stop seeing them every month.

Attached: both run summaries, the diff from #4412, the two files it touched, the
file the 18 live in, one of the test files, and our config. I am not a mutation
testing person and I do
not want to become one — I want to know what number honestly goes on that
checklist on Tuesday, and what I should be doing to the code before then.
